Toward a Multidimensional CDI-CAT: Noun/Predicate Bias in Spanish (Mexican)

George Kachergis

2026-09-19

Motivation

Fourth replication of the noun/predicate bifactor CAT pipeline (Japanese: multidim/; Cantonese: multidim_cantonese/; English: multidim_english/), on Spanish (Mexican) – pulled directly from Wordbank via wordbankr, using the shared pipeline (multidim_pipeline/lib.R) throughout, including the two fixes made along the way (an imputed-vs-raw-matrix bug in the CAT loop, and a vector-min_items bug in the criteria-comparison step – both caught and fixed during this replication, see multidim_pipeline/lib.R history).

items <- read_csv(here("multidim_spanish/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
efa_loadings <- read_csv(here("multidim_spanish/efa2_loadings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_items <- read_csv(here("multidim_spanish/bifactor_item_params.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_spanish/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
cat_summary <- read_csv(here("multidim_spanish/cat_simulation_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_spanish/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))

jp_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
can_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
en_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
en_resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_english/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))
can_resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_cantonese/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))

1. Data and item classification

Spanish (Mexican) WS has 1682 administrations on Wordbank; after excluding 21 non-producers and 45 children at ceiling, 1616 remain – comparable in scale to Cantonese, so (unlike English) the full sample was used directly for every fitting step, no subsampling needed.

Item classification uses the same category → class mapping as the other three languages, plus two Spanish-specific categories (prepositions, states, both mapped to function_word; states has only 3 items). The resulting content-word bank is 478 items (312 noun, 166 predicate) – numerically identical to Japanese and English, the expected result since all three descend from the same source CDI.

items %>%
  count(lexical_class, pos2) %>%
  arrange(pos2) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Lexical class", "CAT dimension (pos2)", "N items"),
        caption = "Spanish item counts by lexical class and CAT grouping.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Spanish item counts by lexical class and CAT grouping.
Lexical class CAT dimension (pos2) N items

function_word other 102
other other 100

2. Exploratory factor check

ggplot(efa_loadings, aes(x = F1, y = F2, color = pos2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "F1 (general)", y = "F2 (noun vs. predicate)", color = "Item type",
       title = "Spanish: exploratory 2-factor loadings") +
  theme_bw()

Fourth replication of the same signature: dominant general factor (mean F1 = 0.77 nouns, 0.81 predicates), a smaller but highly reliable noun/predicate-separating F2 (noun mean 0.108, predicate mean -0.18; Welch t = 29.6, p < .0001), and clean F1/F2 orthogonality (r = 0.016, in between Japanese’s -0.015 and Cantonese’s 0.234).

3. Confirmatory bifactor model

bifactor_items %>%
  mutate(own_specific = if_else(pos2 == "noun", S1_noun, S2_predicate)) %>%
  group_by(pos2) %>%
  summarise(mean_G = mean(G), mean_own_specific = mean(own_specific), n = n()) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.
pos2 mean_G mean_own_specific n
noun 2.33 1.39 312
predicate 2.61 1.65 166

This fit converged cleanly with no warnings – unlike English, which raised a mild “log-likelihood decreasing” warning (later shown not to be consequential via a downstream CAT check).

rel <- empirical_rxx(bifactor_scores %>%
                        select(G, S1_noun, S2_predicate, SE_G, SE_S1_noun, SE_S2_predicate) %>%
                        as.matrix())
tibble(dimension = names(rel), empirical_rxx = rel) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores.
dimension empirical_rxx
G 0.96
S1_noun 0.89
S2_predicate 0.85

Best specific-factor reliability of all four languages (S1 = .89, S2 = .85, vs. Cantonese’s previous best of .86/.80).

ggplot(bifactor_scores, aes(x = production, y = noun_predicate_bias)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Total production (sum score)", y = "Noun/predicate bias (S1 - S2)",
       title = sprintf("r = %.3f", cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias))) +
  theme_bw()

The bias score decouples from vocabulary size more cleanly here than in any other language: r = -0.007 with production (Japanese: -.16, Cantonese: -.11, English: .04) and r = -0.1 with age. The S1/S2 EAP score correlation is 0.66.

4. CAT simulation

Applying the lesson learned from Cantonese and English directly this time – rather than rediscovering it with a “forced longer” follow-up run – min_items was set to ~75% of each length’s ceiling from the start, and min_SEM computed from this dataset’s own full-bank SE ceiling. This worked on the first attempt (after fixing a min_items-vector bug the attempt surfaced in multidim_pipeline/lib.R, see script comments).

cat_summary %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Spanish CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Spanish CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision.
criteria max_items mean_n_items mean_SE_G mean_SE_S1 mean_SE_S2 r_bias_vs_full r_G_vs_full n_items_never_used
Drule 100 92.194 0.234 0.368 0.427 0.944 0.988 73
Drule 200 174.845 0.210 0.338 0.391 0.974 0.995 1
Drule 300 259.480 0.200 0.324 0.376 0.987 0.997 0

Best recovery of all four languages: r = .99 at a 300-item cap (259 items administered on average), and only 1 of 478 items was never selected across the whole simulated sample at that budget – the CAT is using nearly the entire bank.

5. Four-language comparison

tibble(
  language = c("Japanese", "Cantonese", "English (American)", "Spanish (Mexican)"),
  n_for_modeling = c(nrow(jp_bifactor_scores), nrow(can_bifactor_scores), nrow(en_bifactor_scores), nrow(bifactor_scores)),
  n_available = c(nrow(jp_bifactor_scores), nrow(can_resp_data$d_demo), nrow(en_resp_data$d_demo), nrow(resp_data$d_demo)),
  n_content_items = c(478, 572, 478, 478),
  full_bank_reliability_S1 = c(0.71, 0.86, 0.81, 0.89),
  full_bank_reliability_S2 = c(0.64, 0.80, 0.75, 0.85),
  bias_vs_production_r = c(
    round(cor(jp_bifactor_scores$production, jp_bifactor_scores$S1_noun - jp_bifactor_scores$S2_predicate), 2),
    round(cor(can_bifactor_scores$production, can_bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 2),
    round(cor(en_bifactor_scores$production, en_bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 3),
    round(cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 3)
  ),
  best_cat_recovery_r = c(0.95, 0.97, 0.98, 0.99),
  items_for_best_recovery = c(131, 192, 257, 259)
) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Japanese vs. Cantonese vs. English vs. Spanish: key numbers side by side.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

The bifactor design and Drule-based CAT transfer cleanly across all four languages tested, with Spanish giving the strongest results on every metric: highest specific-factor reliability, tightest bias/vocabulary-size decoupling, and best CAT recovery. The engineering also matured across the four replications – Spanish is the first language where the full pipeline (prep through CAT simulation) ran correctly without needing a follow-up “forced longer” or bug-fix run during the CAT stage itself (one min_items-vector bug was caught and fixed in multidim_pipeline/lib.R before the successful run, rather than being discovered via a bad result afterward).

A related question was tested and resolved during this replication (on Japanese): whether a genuinely 2-dimensional model (G + a single bipolar noun-vs-predicate contrast, instead of two orthogonal specific factors subtracted post-hoc) might be a cleaner alternative. Two independent fit attempts (default and EFA-informed starting values) both failed to converge to a sensible solution – G loadings diverged to implausible magnitudes (-1 to -21) and the Bias dimension lost its bipolar character. This appears to be a structural estimation problem (G and Bias sharing the exact same item set with no “pure G” anchor items), not a fixable numerical fluke, so the current 2-group bifactor design (bias = S1-S2) remains the recommended approach; see multidim_pipeline/bias_dimensionality_comparison.R and bias_1group_refit_with_starts.R for the full investigation.

6. Open questions

  1. A cross-linguistic item-overlap analysis (multidim_pipeline/cross_linguistic_item_overlap.R) is being extended to include Spanish: do the same concepts (uni_lemma) turn out to be the most discriminating items for the noun/predicate dimension across all four languages? Preliminary 3-language results (before Spanish) showed strong cross-linguistic transfer for nouns but much weaker (and for Japanese, below-chance) transfer for predicates – echoing Hagihara et al.’s own finding that verb/adjective bias is more cross-linguistically variable than noun bias.
  2. English used a documented n=1500 subsample given its much larger available sample (~9000); Spanish and Cantonese used their full samples directly. Worth deciding whether a full-sample English refit is warranted given how promising the subsampled results already are.
  3. Given the min_items floor needed for good recovery (150-250+ across all four languages) is much longer than the existing unidimensional production CATs (~25-50 items), the combined-vs-separate administration question (raised in the English write-up) remains open across all four languages.
